title: Financial Risk
description: The financial risk test determines whether U.S. contractors performing research for clients can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41.
summary: The financial risk test determines whether U.S. contractors performing research for clients can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. Under the funded research exclusion, payment must be contingent on technical success, not effort expended, and the contractor must also retain substantial rights in the results; otherwise the research is funded and ineligible.

body.text: The financial risk test determines whether U.S. contractors performing research for clients can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. Under the funded research exclusion, payment must be contingent on technical success, not effort expended, and the contractor must also retain substantial rights in the results; otherwise the research is funded and ineligible.
Executive Summary and the Statutory Role of Financial Risk

The federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit, codified under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (IRC § 41), provides a dollar-for-dollar reduction in corporate tax liability calculated from Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) incurred in the design, development, or improvement of products, processes, techniques, formulas, inventions, or software. While the credit serves as a primary fiscal mechanism for incentivizing domestic technological investment and preserving corporate cash flow, eligibility requires strict adherence to both the statutory Four-Part Test and a series of statutory exclusions. Among these statutory limitations, the "Funded Research" exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) represents a frequent basis for Internal Revenue Service (IRS) audit adjustments and credit disallowances, particularly for taxpayers operating under government contracts or third-party commercial development agreements.

Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), qualified research explicitly excludes any research to the extent that it is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or any governmental entity. To operationalize this statutory mandate, Treasury Regulations establish a mandatory two-pronged standard—comprising the Risk Standard (Financial Risk) and the Substantial Rights Standard (Intellectual Property Rights)—which a taxpayer must satisfy concurrently for contracted research expenditures to qualify as unfunded. Although practitioner analyses occasionally reference Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) as the codification of this two-pronged funded research standard, within the formal regulatory architecture of IRC § 41, the funded research rules governing financial risk and substantial rights are codified at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), as expressly cross-referenced by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9), operating alongside the contract research payment contingency rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e).

From an analytical and tax compliance perspective, the allocation of financial risk within inter-party contracts dictates not only the availability of the R&D tax credit under IRC § 41, but also the taxpayer's broader exposure to examination adjustments and statutory penalties. When the IRS disallows claimed QREs because the underlying agreements fail to establish that the contractor bore the economic risk of technical failure, the disallowance frequently exposes wider deficiencies in contemporaneous project-level substantiation. As reflected in recent U.S. Tax Court enforcement trends—including the Phoenix Design litigation—insufficient contractual and technical documentation can trigger accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662. Consequently, engineering precise payment contingencies and maintaining integrated documentation of financial risk are essential prerequisites for defending R&D tax credit claims against administrative challenge.

The strategic importance of the funded research exclusion stems from its function as a statutory anti-double-dipping and capital-at-risk rule. In bilateral commercial or governmental research arrangements, two distinct corporate taxpayers—the funding client and the performing contractor—frequently interact over the same technological development scope. If a funding client pays a contractor on a guaranteed cost-reimbursement basis, the client bears the financial risk of experimental failure and may potentially claim 65 percent of the payments as contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), whereas the contractor is insulated from loss and barred from claiming in-house QREs under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). Conversely, when the contractor assumes genuine financial exposure by conditioning its right to compensation on the successful resolution of technological uncertainty, the economic burden shifts to the performer. Understanding this bilateral equilibrium is vital for corporate tax departments, as ambiguous contract drafting can inadvertently create a fiscal deadweight loss in which neither party satisfies the regulatory prerequisites to claim the credit.
Definitional Foundation and Regulatory Mechanics of the Financial Risk Standard
The Payment Contingency Requirement

In the statutory and regulatory framework of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), financial risk is defined by the contingency of compensation relative to technical outcomes. For research expenses incurred by a contractor or research performer to be treated as unfunded, the amounts payable under the governing agreement must be explicitly contingent upon the success of the research. The regulatory standard distinguishes sharply between compensation paid for the successful achievement of a specified technical product or result and compensation paid merely for the expenditure of labor hours, materials, or effort. To bear financial risk, the performing taxpayer must face a substantive economic exposure, defined as the genuine legal and financial possibility of incurring research costs without reimbursement—or being legally obligated to refund progress payments—if the research fails to satisfy the customer's or funder's technical specifications.

Furthermore, evaluating the true allocation of economic burden requires examining the entirety of the commercial relationship rather than reviewing a single formal statement of work in isolation. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the funded research inquiry must encompass all agreements, side letters, bilateral modifications, and course-of-dealing arrangements between the taxpayer and other parties. Whenever an agreement guarantees reimbursement for the researcher's incurred costs irrespective of the technical outcome—as is characteristic of standard cost-reimbursement arrangements—the economic burden of potential experimental failure resides with the funding customer rather than the researcher. Under such terms, the research is legally classified as "funded," disqualifying the performing contractor from including those expenditures in its QRE calculation.

This holistic evaluation of all inter-party agreements prevents taxpayers from relying on cosmetic fixed-price labels while eliminating economic exposure through secondary commercial mechanisms. For example, if a master services agreement (MSA) contains a broad indemnification or termination-for-convenience provision that obligates the client to reimburse all incurred direct labor and material costs plus a standard markup regardless of whether any technical milestone was achieved, an IRS examiner reviewing the integrated contract file will treat the arrangement as guaranteed cost recovery. Similarly, a practice of routinely executing upward change orders whenever experimental difficulties arise undermines the assertion that the original fixed price placed the contractor's capital at risk. True payment contingency demands that the contractor's legal entitlement to receive and retain revenue remains bound to verifiable technical performance throughout the life of the engagement.
Analytical Interplay Between Financial Risk and Technical Uncertainty

Beyond its direct exclusionary function under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), the Financial Risk Standard serves an important corroborative role in substantiating the technical elements of the R&D credit. The underlying fiscal policy objective of IRC § 41 is to incentivize a taxpayer's deployment of its own capital at risk to resolve technological uncertainty through a systematic process of experimentation. If a counterparty insulates the researcher from financial loss via a guaranteed cost-recovery mechanism, the statutory incentive rationale is neutralized as to the contractor.

More critically, from an audit-defense standpoint, the pricing and risk structure of a contract acts as an objective market signal regarding the presence of technical uncertainty under the Four-Part Test. When a customer agrees to pay a contractor unconditionally for time and materials without tying payment to technical acceptance criteria, examiners may infer that neither party perceived significant technological uncertainty in the outcome, or that the client retained full technical direction and risk over the developmental effort. Conversely, a contract containing strict technical acceptance milestones, explicit rejection rights, and contractor-funded rework obligations corroborates the taxpayer's assertion that the underlying work involved genuine technical uncertainty concerning capability, methodology, or appropriate design and required systematic experimentation.

This structural linkage between IRC § 41(d)(1) (the Four-Part Test) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) (the Funded Research Exclusion) carries profound implications for audit strategy. During an IRS examination, engineering specialists and revenue agents evaluate whether the claimed uncertainties were technological in nature rather than mere scheduling, aesthetic, or commercial uncertainties. When contractual payment milestones are drafted solely around calendar delivery dates or generic phase completions without reference to quantitative performance thresholds, the taxpayer faces a dual vulnerability: the contract fails to prove that payment was contingent on research success under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), and simultaneously fails to provide contemporaneous commercial evidence that the project aimed to resolve technical uncertainty under IRC § 41(d)(1). Aligning contractual acceptance metrics with engineering parameters therefore reinforces both prongs of statutory eligibility simultaneously.
The Two-Prong Unfunded Research Framework: Interdependence of Risk and Rights

To avoid classification as funded research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), a taxpayer performing research under contract must satisfy both prongs of the regulatory test. Failure on either prong renders the associated expenditures funded and therefore ineligible for the credit.

The taxpayer performing the research must not retain "no substantial rights" in the resulting research product.

body.text: Prong 1: Substantial Performance and Warranty of Results

Under the Risk Standard analysis—addressed in administrative guidance such as IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20223401F—contractual payment is considered contingent on research success when the agreement mandates substantial performance of technical objectives or incorporates a warranty of results. Notably, where a contract is governed by state or local law that implies or imposes a warranty-of-results standard, that governing legal framework can reinforce the taxpayer's position that payment is legally contingent upon successful technical delivery. Establishing this prong requires a granular review of contractual clauses governing deliverable inspection, technical rejection, cure periods, and payment withholding upon technical failure.

However, reliance on implied state-law doctrines of substantial performance requires careful distinction between ordinary professional negligence standards and an actual warranty of technical results. In many jurisdictions, standard commercial contracts for engineering or architectural services only obligate the service provider to exercise a professional standard of care, meaning the provider is entitled to compensation for services rendered even if an experimental design proves technically unfeasible, provided the work was performed without negligence. To satisfy the Risk Standard under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the contract—either through its express terms or the specific operation of governing law—must condition the right to compensation on the successful achievement of the technical result itself, rather than mere adherence to professional workmanship standards. Explicit contractual provisions detailing formal acceptance testing, client rejection rights, and uncompensated remediation obligations remain the most durable evidence of payment contingency.
Prong 2: Retention of Substantial Intellectual Property Rights

Satisfying the Financial Risk Standard is a necessary but insufficient condition for claiming QREs on contracted projects. Under the Substantial Rights Standard of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)-(3), even where a contractor assumes the entirety of the financial risk of failure, the research remains "funded" if the contractor retains "no substantial rights" in the findings or product of the research. This requirement ensures that the taxpayer claiming the credit possesses the legal capacity to commercially utilize the innovations generated by the at-risk research without having to pay a royalty or obtain permission from the counterparty on terms equivalent to an unrelated third party. For instance, a government contractor developing proprietary software for a federal agency can satisfy the Substantial Rights Standard by retaining non-exclusive rights to deploy the underlying software architecture, routines, or algorithms in commercial products outside the scope of the government contract.

Conversely, incidental benefits gained by performing the research—such as increased general workforce experience, enhanced market reputation, or the right to bid on future production contracts—do not constitute substantial rights in the research findings under the regulations. The contractor must retain a legally enforceable right to use the actual technical developments, inventions, or trade secrets produced during the engagement.
The Joint Operation of Risk and Rights

A recurring compliance vulnerability in third-party R&D contracting is the contractual decoupling of economic risk from intellectual property ownership. Because the two regulatory standards operate conjunctively, a corporate taxpayer that assumes full economic exposure under a Firm Fixed Price contract—absorbing all cost overruns and conditioning payment on strict technical performance—will nevertheless forfeit the R&D tax credit if the contract assigns exclusive ownership of all resulting IP to the client without preserving substantial usage rights for the contractor.

Moreover, asymmetric allocation of risk and rights across contracting parties can result in an "orphan credit" scenario under the combined operation of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). If a contractor performs research under a fixed-price contract where payment is contingent on technical success (placing financial risk on the contractor), but the client demands exclusive ownership of all resulting intellectual property and prohibits the contractor from reusing the technology (stripping the contractor of substantial rights), the contractor is disqualified under the Substantial Rights Standard. At the same time, the client is barred from claiming contract research expenses under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2) because the client's payments were contingent upon the success of the research, meaning the client did not bear the financial risk of failure. Tax planning and contract negotiation must therefore treat financial risk clauses and IP licensing provisions as an integrated compliance unit.
Contractual Mechanisms and Quantitative Modeling of Financial Risk Allocation
Comparative Analysis of Standard Contract Archetypes

The baseline allocation of financial risk in third-party R&D engagements is heavily influenced by the underlying contract pricing structure. Drawing upon standard commercial and government procurement classifications—such as those defined by the Defense Acquisition University (DAU)—agreements can be categorized along a spectrum of contractor cost responsibility encompassing Firm Fixed Price (FFP), Cost Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF), and Time and Materials (T&M) structures.

In a Firm Fixed Price (FFP) arrangement, the contractor commits to delivering a specified technical scope for a predetermined price. Because the contract price is not subject to upward adjustment based on the contractor's actual cost experience, the contractor absorbs all cost overruns resulting from unexpected experimental failures and bears the primary financial risk. When FFP payments are tied to verifiable technical milestones requiring customer acceptance of research results, the structure generally supports R&D credit eligibility for the contractor.

By contrast, under a Cost Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF) structure, the funding customer or government agency reimburses the contractor for all allowable incurred costs up to pre-established ceilings and pays an additional fixed fee. Because the funder bears the performance cost risk and the contractor is insulated from the financial loss of research failure, CPFF contracts reduce the contractor's financial exposure and are generally deemed "funded" and ineligible for the contractor. Similarly, Time and Materials (T&M) contracts compensate the contractor based on direct labor hours expended at fixed hourly billing rates plus the actual cost of materials utilized. Because T&M compensation tracks effort expended rather than the successful resolution of technical uncertainty, the customer assumes the financial risk. Unless modified by an enforceable price cap paired with a strict technical performance guarantee requiring uncompensated rework, T&M contracts attract heightened IRS examination scrutiny and generally fail the Financial Risk Standard for the contractor.

body.text: Worked Hypothetical Case Study: Firm Fixed Price Overrun Absorption

To illustrate how fixed-price structures establish financial risk retention in practice, consider a chemical manufacturing scenario involving "Company C" and "Client D". In this baseline engagement, Company C enters into a Firm Fixed Price contract with Client D for a total fixed price of $750,000 to develop a novel, cost-efficient chemical catalyst formulation requiring substantial experimentation. The contract explicitly mandates that final payment of the $750,000 price is contingent upon the newly developed catalyst achieving and sustaining a minimum conversion rate of 95% during pilot testing, an outcome that is technically uncertain at contract inception.

During the execution of the research, unexpected technical failures force Company C to conduct extensive re-experimentation, resulting in total incurred QREs (comprising direct labor and experimental materials) of $900,000. Recomputing the financial outcome confirms that because the contract price is capped at $750,000, Company C must absorb the uncompensated cost overrun directly:
Absorbed Cost Overrun = Total Incurred QREs − Fixed Contract Price = $900,000 − $750,000 = $150,000
Expressed as a proportion of the negotiated contract ceiling, Company C absorbs a 20.0% negative cost variance on its own books:

Because Company C's legal right to receive the $750,000 contract price was conditioned upon achieving the 95% conversion rate, and because Company C bore the entirety of the $150,000 overrun caused by technical failure, the economic burden of experimental uncertainty rested on Company C. Assuming Company C also satisfies the Substantial Rights Standard, it is eligible to claim the full $900,000 of incurred QREs rather than merely the $150,000 uncompensated overrun.

This distinction between total at-risk expenditures ($900,000) and net out-of-pocket loss ($150,000) illustrates a crucial regulatory principle under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). When payments under a contract are contingent upon the success of the research, the entire research project is treated as unfunded, even after the contractor successfully achieves the technical milestone and receives the $750,000 contract price. In other words, the tax law evaluates financial risk ex ante based on the legal contingency of the payment obligation during the conduct of the research, rather than limiting QREs ex post to unprofitable contracts. Conversely, if Client D had guaranteed reimbursement of the first $750,000 regardless of whether the 95% conversion rate was met, and only capped its reimbursement at $750,000, the first $750,000 would be disallowed as funded research under the "to the extent funded" language of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), leaving only the excess $150,000 potentially eligible as unfunded QREs.
Parametric Analysis of Contractual Risk Clauses (Hypothetical $100,000 Contract Model)

In addition to qualitative contract comparisons, an analytical simulation model (the R&D Tax Credit Financial Risk Analyzer) demonstrates how individual contractual provisions interact to shift financial exposure between the client and the contractor on a hypothetical $100,000 R&D contract. While internal scoring rubrics function as analytical heuristics for pre-audit risk assessment rather than statutory safe harbors, evaluating the mathematical model clarifies the relative weight tax practitioners assign to specific contract clauses:
Risk Retention Score = S<sub>structure</sub> + S<sub>acceptance</sub> + S<sub>warranty</sub> + S<sub>liability</sub>

Within this quantitative framework, four contractual variables determine whether the contractor meets the modeled 60% (60 points) Risk Retention Score threshold required to claim the $100,000 QRE basis. The first variable, Payment Structure (Sstructure, carrying a maximum weight of 40 points), scales linearly based on the fixed-price ratio (rfixed ∈ [0%, 100%]) according to Sstructure = 40 × rfixed, ranging from 0% fixed price for pure hourly T&M arrangements (contributing 0 points), through Hybrid or Capped arrangements where rfixed falls between 1% and 99% (such as 50%, contributing 20 points), up to 100% for pure Fixed Price arrangements (contributing the full 40 points). The second variable, the Acceptance Clause indicator (Sacceptance, weighted at 30 points), awards 30 points if the client must formally inspect and approve technical deliverables against specified criteria before payment is earned, and 0 points if no acceptance condition applies. The third variable, Warranty and Rework Responsibility (Swarranty, weighted at 20 points), awards 20 points if the contractor must remediate bugs, defects, or technical failures at its own expense ("Contractor Pays"), compared to 0 points if defect remediation is billable to the client. Finally, the fourth variable, Liability Cap Exposure (Sliability, weighted at 10 points), awards 10 points when the contractor's financial exposure for non-performance is unlimited ("No Cap"), and 0 points when contractual liability is capped.

body.text: A critical analytical finding emerges from comparing Scenario 2 and Scenario 3 in the modeled calculations. Even when a contract is nominally labeled "Fixed Price" (100%, yielding 40 points) with uncapped liability (10 points), the absence of an explicit client acceptance clause (0 points) and the ability to bill the client separately for warranty or rework (0 points) leaves the contractor at a 50% score—failing the 60% eligibility threshold. Conversely, a hybrid or capped contract (50%, yielding 20 points) that enforces strict client acceptance (30 points) and requires the contractor to pay for all defect remediation (20 points) achieves a 70% score and qualifies the $100,000 QRE basis. This quantitative relationship mirrors the exact judicial trajectory in modern Section 41 jurisprudence, wherein substantive acceptance and rework clauses outweigh nominal contract labels.
Judicial Interpretation and Precedent: From Fairchild to Modern Substantive Scrutiny
The Controlling Precedent: Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States

The foundational judicial interpretation of the Financial Risk Standard was established in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States (docket No. 94-5116). In Fairchild, an aerospace manufacturer entered into a fixed-price incentive contract with the U.S. Air Force for the design and production of the T-46A next-generation trainer aircraft. During the course of performance, Fairchild received progress payments from the Air Force, prompting the government to argue that the research was "funded" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) to the extent of those progress disbursements.

The court rejected the government's position and held that Fairchild's research expenditures were not funded. Focusing narrowly on the legal allocation of the costs of failure, the court concluded that Fairchild's right to retain any payments under the contract was strictly conditioned upon delivering work that met the Air Force's detailed technical specifications for the T-46A aircraft. Because the contract granted the Air Force the explicit right to inspect deliverables, reject non-conforming work, and require Fairchild to correct technical deficiencies at its own expense—or refund unliquidated progress payments if the contract was terminated for default—the contractor bore the financial risk of failed research. Fairchild thus established the enduring rule that the receipt of interim progress payments during performance does not automatically render research "funded," provided the contractor's ultimate legal entitlement to retain those funds remains contingent upon successful technical delivery.
Modern Tax Court Scrutiny and the Shift to Substantive Contingency

While Fairchild remains the touchstone precedent for fixed-price government contractors, recent U.S. Tax Court opinions have significantly tightened judicial scrutiny over commercial design, architecture, engineering, and software contracts. Rather than accepting a contract's designation as "Firm Fixed Price" or "lump sum" at face value, modern courts examine the substantive operative language of the agreement to verify whether payment is genuinely contingent upon the success of the underlying research itself—defined as the resolution of technological uncertainty—as opposed to the mere delivery of a standard professional service or serviceable commercial product.

In phased engineering or architectural contracts, general client sign-offs at the end of schematic design, design development, or construction document phases frequently fail to satisfy modern judicial scrutiny if the contractor is entitled to keep payments for completed phases regardless of whether the final integrated design achieves its experimental objectives. Instead, courts increasingly demand specific contractual riders that link financial failure directly to experimental failure through three mutually reinforcing contractual mechanisms. First, agreements must incorporate objective technical acceptance metrics, defined as quantifiable performance criteria directly tied to uncertain R&D parameters rather than general commercial deliverables or scheduling milestones. Second, contracts must include explicit refund or clawback clauses establishing binding legal obligations that require the return of prior milestone or progress payments if the experimental deliverable fails final acceptance testing. Third, agreements must enforce unambiguous rework and penalty provisions obligating the contractor to absorb all costs of re-engineering failed prototypes or designs without upward adjustment to the contract price.

This doctrinal evolution reflects a judicial recognition that commercial service contracts differ structurally from military hardware procurement agreements like the T-46A contract in Fairchild. In Fairchild, the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) default, inspection, and progress-payment liquidation clauses automatically subordinated every interim disbursement to the final technical delivery of a functioning aircraft prototype. In private-sector architectural, engineering, and software engagements, standard industry form contracts typically provide for progressive invoicing upon periodic percentage-of-completion milestones, coupled with termination clauses that entitle the consultant to payment for all work performed up to the date of termination. When a taxpayer relies on such standard industry agreements without adding explicit technical acceptance and clawback provisions, the contractor is legally entitled to retain interim payments even if subsequent experimental phases fail, thereby shifting the financial risk of earlier stages onto the client and rendering the research funded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
Audit Defense, Substantiation Standards, and Regulatory Reform Recommendations
Contemporaneous Documentation and IRS Examination Posture

Defending the Financial Risk Standard under IRS examination requires a dual-track substantiation strategy that bridges legal contract analysis and project cost accounting. As highlighted in administrative guidance such as IRS Chief Counsel Memoranda 20214101F and 20223401F, technical activity records—such as engineering logs, test results, and commit histories used to prove the Four-Part Test—are insufficient on their own when research is performed for third parties. Taxpayers must maintain a complete, contemporaneous evidentiary trail of all financial and legal instruments governing the project, including master services agreements (MSAs), statements of work (SOWs), bilateral contract modifications, change orders, milestone acceptance certificates, and billing invoices.

To minimize audit exposure and prevent the imposition of IRC § 6662 accuracy-related penalties, corporate taxpayers must implement three interconnected contractual and accounting practices. First, taxpayers intending to claim R&D credits must eliminate guaranteed cost-recovery mechanisms—such as pure T&M or generic CPFF contracts—for experimental workstreams, as these structures transfer economic risk to the customer and presumptively disqualify the contractor. Where a client relationship involves both routine implementation services and high-uncertainty R&D, separating the experimental scope into a distinct, fixed-price SOW with strict acceptance contingencies prevents the T&M billing structure of the routine work from tainting the R&D project. Second, all fixed-price contracts should integrate explicit failure, rejection, and rework clauses ensuring that the contractor is legally responsible for absorbing the costs of rework or non-performance if defined technical specifications are not achieved. Third, contractual billing milestones and acceptance criteria must be synchronized with technical R&D uncertainties so that invoice triggers correspond directly to the resolution of technical uncertainties under the IRC § 41 Four-Part Test, while project cost-accounting systems simultaneously track unbilled rework hours and cost overruns at the business-component level to provide examiners with direct quantitative proof that the contractor bore financial risk in practice.
Analysis of Recommendations for IRS and Treasury Regulatory Clarification

Significant ambiguity persists in applying the traditional Fairchild tangible-product framework to modern, iterative R&D environments such as complex software engineering, where the deliverable is frequently an algorithm, cloud architecture, or body of technical knowledge rather than a discrete physical prototype. To resolve these compliance disputes and reduce examination friction, a four-part administrative and regulatory reform agenda is warranted for the IRS and the Treasury Department.

First, the IRS should publish a formal Revenue Ruling or industry-specific guidance defining what constitutes "research success" across iterative development lifecycles (such as Agile software engineering), clarifying specifically when interim payments tied to project phases or software sprints qualify as contingent payments for technical results rather than non-contingent funding for effort expended. Second, the Treasury Department should refine the regulatory language governing funded research and "substantial performance" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) (and its cross-reference in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9)) to distinguish clearly between routine commercial warranties of operational stability—which do not satisfy the Risk Standard—and true warranties of technical results linked to resolving underlying technological uncertainty, thereby aligning administrative rules with strict Tax Court precedent.

Third, to reduce subjective contract interpretation during IRS examinations, the Treasury Department should establish quantitative safe harbors for fixed-price and hybrid agreements. Under an illustrative safe harbor framework, an FFP contract that allocates a minimum specified percentage—such as 75%—of the total contract payment to milestones explicitly contingent upon achieving documented technical specifications that resolve uncertainty would be treated as prima facie compliant with the Financial Risk Standard. Applying this 75% safe harbor to the earlier $750,000 FFP contract baseline demonstrates that if at least 75% ($562,500) of the contract price is contingent on technical uncertainty milestones, up to 25% ($187,500) in initial mobilization or interim payments would not taint the unfunded status of the contract:
Minimum Contingent Milestone Allocation = 0.75 × $750,000 = $562,500
Permissible Mobilization / Interim Allocation = 0.25 × $750,000 = $187,500

Fourth and finally, the IRS should update its standard compliance documentation requirements to mandate the simultaneous presentation and cross-referencing of Four-Part Test technical records alongside IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) financial risk documentation, ensuring that taxpayers systematically track cost absorption directly alongside the resolution of experimental uncertainty.
